headline: José Luis Castro: when climate diplomacy fails, our lungs pay the price
dek: After COP31 ended without agreement on the Antalya Pact, the WHO Special Envoy for Chronic Respiratory Diseases called for health outcomes, clean air and respiratory care to be built into climate commitments and adaptation finance before COP32 in Addis Ababa.
body:
José Luis Castro, WHO Director-General Special Envoy for Chronic Respiratory Diseases, wrote in a LinkedIn article that the outcome of COP31 in Antalya will be felt in people's lungs. COP31 closed on 22 November without consensus on the proposed Antalya Pact, with differences over the transition away from fossil fuels and adaptation finance unresolved, although progress was made on the just transition and adaptation indicators. Castro noted that WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus described the outcome as a grave setback for the protection of lives and health, according to press coverage.

Castro argued that cleaner air is one of the fastest returns on climate action. Replacing a diesel bus with an electric one removes tailpipe pollution for the people waiting at the kerb straight away, he wrote, while the climate gains grow as electricity gets cleaner. He cited WHO's estimate that household and ambient air pollution together are associated with around seven million premature deaths a year, and a Southern California study of more than 2,000 children in which lung function improved as fine particle and nitrogen dioxide levels fell.

He also described how a warming climate makes breathing harder: wildfire smoke, ground-level ozone on hot days, longer pollen seasons, dust and extreme heat all weigh on people with asthma, COPD and other lung diseases. A washed-out road can cut off access to an inhaler, he wrote, and a power cut can switch off a home oxygen machine. Most asthma deaths occur in low- and lower-middle-income countries, and the communities that contributed least to global warming face the greatest challenges in protection and care.

On finance, Castro pointed to the gap between international public adaptation finance for developing countries of US$28.2–31.7bn in 2024 and UNEP's estimate that annual needs will reach US$305bn by 2035. He said health had a very prominent place at the summit, and that the challenge now is securing funding for initiatives such as the Belém Health Action Plan, ATACH and the Antalya Initiative for Health Resilience. He cited WHO modelling suggesting that scaling up a set of climate-health interventions globally could avert around 1.6 million deaths a year.

Looking ahead to COP32 in Addis Ababa, Castro called on governments to put health outcomes into climate commitments, measuring pollution by neighbourhood and asthma attacks by age and location. He said adaptation finance should fund prevention, early diagnosis and spirometry in primary care, keep essential inhalers in stock, arrange refills for people displaced by floods or fires, and provide filtered-air spaces with backup power for oxygen equipment. He also pointed to World Health Assembly resolution WHA78.5 on an integrated lung health approach as an opportunity to bring these agendas together.

"Clean air is fundamental to health and to the enjoyment of the human right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment," Castro wrote.
key_quote: Its protection cannot wait for the next round of climate negotiations.
